title: How do you focus on what matters most in a case interview?
description: How to prioritise in a case interview so you spend time on the few factors that drive most of the answer, with examples and phrases.
hook: In most problems, a few causes explain most of the effect. Roughly 80% of the results often come from 20% of the factors. You do not need to apply this precisely; the useful part is the habit of asking "what are the one or two things that matter most here?" In a 30-minute case, that habit is what keeps you from running out of time.
body:
What it looks like in practice

  • Two products make up most of the revenue, so a revenue drop is probably there.
  • Fuel and staff are most of an airline's costs, so a cost case starts there, not with stationery.
  • A handful of large customers may drive most of the profit in a business-to-business company.

How to use it

  1. When you lay out your structure, say which branch is likely to matter most, and why.
  2. When you get a breakdown, look for the biggest pieces first.
  3. When you brainstorm, rank your ideas by impact and focus on the top two or three.

A phrase to use

There are several possible causes, but given that delivery is 40% of costs, I'd start there because it's most likely to explain the change.

A word of caution

Prioritising does not mean ignoring everything else. Mention the smaller areas briefly, then say you will come back to them if time allows. In your recommendation, list them as next steps.

Prioritisation requires evidence, not a magic percentage

Suppose a retailer has ten product lines. Two account for 65% of sales and the remaining eight for 35%. That is a reason to examine the leading products first, but not proof that they explain a profit problem. One of the smaller products might carry most of the margin or have suffered the largest recent decline.

In a case, start with materiality × likelihood × decision value. A cost line worth £40 million is material; a 2% increase on it contributes £800,000. A £2 million cost line rising by 50% contributes £1 million. Looking only at the largest baseline would miss the bigger movement in the smaller line.

Use the 80/20 idea as a reminder to spend limited interview time on what can explain the client's objective. Quantify the contribution, check what has actually changed, and keep one alternative hypothesis alive. There is no universal requirement that exactly 80% of impact comes from 20% of causes.
